explanation: It began as a hardware quirk: with fewer aliens to draw, the processor moved the survivors more quickly. Its designer, Tomohiro Nishikado, liked the rising tension and kept it.

claims.text: In Space Invaders, released in 1978, the remaining invaders speed up as more of them are destroyed.
In Space Invaders, shot aliens do not make the others split in two, change colour or stop firing.
The speed-up came from the hardware: with fewer aliens to draw on screen, the game could move the rest faster.
Space Invaders was designed by Tomohiro Nishikado, who kept the speed-up as a feature because it raised the tension.

evidence.restatement: Taito's 1978 arcade game makes the surviving aliens march more quickly the fewer of them are left.

claimResults.note: Answered cold. Space Invaders came out in Japan in 1978 (Taito), and the accelerating formation is its defining mechanic.

evidence.restatement: Destroying invaders never makes the rest divide, recolour or cease shooting; they only speed up.

claimResults.note: Splitting is an Asteroids mechanic, a nice plausible lure. The cabinet's colour came from fixed cellophane overlay bands, which do not change with kills, so 'change colour' is wrong as a response to picking them off. All three definitely wrong.

evidence.restatement: The acceleration was an accident of the limited hardware: each frame had fewer sprites to render, so the remaining aliens moved more often.

claimResults.note: Nishikado's own often-repeated account of the game's development.

evidence.restatement: Tomohiro Nishikado created Space Invaders and chose to leave the accidental speed-up in because it built tension.

claimResults.note: Matches Nishikado's interviews; attribution of the design to him is uncontested.

evidence.restatement: Taito's 1978 arcade game makes the surviving aliens march faster each time one is destroyed, ending with a single very fast invader.

claimResults.note: The speed-up is the defining mechanic of the game. Date 1978 is the arcade release year (Japan, June 1978). No other version of the game reverses the effect.

evidence.restatement: Aliens in the original arcade game never split, never recolour as their numbers fall and keep firing right to the end.

claimResults.note: Rival test on each distractor. The coloured bands on the original screen are a fixed cellophane overlay by screen zone, not a reaction to kills, so 'change colour' is not a defensible second answer. Aliens keep dropping bombs until destroyed or the player dies.

evidence.restatement: The acceleration was a side effect of the processor having less to redraw as aliens vanished, so it ran the loop faster.

claimResults.note: Matches Nishikado's own account, widely repeated.

evidence.restatement: Nishikado created the game, noticed the unplanned speed-up, and chose to leave it in because it made the late stage tenser.

claimResults.note: Designer attribution and the keep-it decision are standard history.

stem: In Space Invaders, what happens to the invaders still on screen as the player picks off more of them?
